explain.say: Picture a group project. One person yells orders. Another asks everyone for ideas, then helps the group decide. Who would you rather follow? Look at the board. Let us sort good leadership from just being bossy.

explain.say: See the first group, good leader? A good leader listens to everyone, sets an example by working hard, and shares the credit when things go well. Leadership means helping a group reach a goal together. Who is a good leader you know?

explain.say: Now look at just bossy. Giving orders, grabbing the credit and blaming others may look like leading, but people stop trying when they are treated like that. A title alone does not make a leader. Have you ever worked with someone bossy? How did it feel?

explain.say: Look at the good leader group again: owns mistakes and helps others grow. Great leaders say sorry when they get it wrong, and give others chances to lead too. Nelson Mandela compared leading to a shepherd who lets the flock go ahead. Why might that work?

explain.say: And here is the best part: you do not need to be in charge to lead. Picking up litter first, or including someone left out, is leadership too. Well done! Challenge: find one small way to lead by example tomorrow.

faq.a: A good leader listens, sets an example, treats people fairly, shares credit, owns mistakes and helps the group reach a goal together. Good leaders make others feel able to contribute.
They listen to everyone, explain the goal, set an example, encourage others, share the credit and help team members grow.

faq.q: What is the difference between a leader and a boss?
faq.a: A boss has power and may just give orders. A leader earns people's trust, so they want to follow. A person can be both, or a leader without any title.
Yes. Leadership is about actions, not titles. Anyone can lead by setting an example, speaking up for others or starting something good.
asks: Do you have to be in charge to lead?

faq.q: Why should a leader own their mistakes?
faq.a: When leaders admit mistakes, the group trusts them more and feels safe to try new things without fear of blame. It also teaches everyone to learn from errors.
asks: Why do good leaders admit mistakes?

facts: In his autobiography "Long Walk to Freedom" (1994), Nelson Mandela compared a leader to a shepherd who stays behind the flock.
Google's Project Aristotle study of 180 teams found that "psychological safety", feeling safe to speak up, mattered most for team success.

quiz.why: Listening makes everyone feel valued and brings out the best ideas.

wrong.0: Taking credit makes people feel used.
